question: In a finite sequence space, are globally normalized energy-based sequence models and locally normalized autoregressive next-token models representationally equivalent, and what does that equivalence actually imply about teacher forcing, soft Bellman lookahead, and approximate EBM-to-ARM distillation?

key_findings.claim: The paper constructs an explicit score-function bijection between a decomposed EBM and an ARM, yielding exactly the same sequence distribution in the finite tabular setting.
key_findings.evidence: For sequence reward R_r(x,y)=sum_t r(s_t,y_t), the forward map sets q(s_t,y_t)=r(s_t,y_t)+V_q(s_t concatenated with y_t) before EOS and q=r at EOS; the inverse subtracts the next-state log-partition. Proposition 1 and its telescoping proof give p_EBM_Rr(y|x)=p_ARM_q(y|x) and A_EBM_Rr(x)=V_q(x). This is a bijection between the chosen local score representations, not a statement that a finite causal neural network can efficiently learn every mapped score.

key_findings.claim: The future-value correction in the bijection is exactly a finite-horizon soft Bellman equation and a backward dynamic program on the prefix tree.
key_findings.evidence: Viewing contexts as states and tokens as actions turns the recursion into q=r+gamma E[V_q(next state)] with deterministic transitions and gamma=1. Because the horizon is finite and acyclic, backward induction gives an explicit unique solution rather than iterative fixed-point convergence. The same quantity is the backward variable log beta in the probabilistic-inference derivation, so the ARM next-token probability combines immediate potential with the total soft value of all continuations.

key_findings.claim: Exact conversion is directionally asymmetric: an ARM score can be converted to a local EBM score in linear sequence cost, whereas explicit EBM-to-ARM conversion is exponential.
key_findings.evidence: The inverse r=M^-1(q) only needs each next-state log-partition and costs O(VT), while computing q=M(r) requires marginalizing every continuation in a V-ary prefix tree and costs O(V^T). The paper's practical teacher-forcing argument therefore relies on learning the ARM implicitly from data, not on executing the exact EBM-to-ARM map for an LLM-sized space.

anchors.section: A.9 Difference with HMMs and CRFs

key_findings.claim: At the level of unconstrained score functions, EBM and ARM negative-log-likelihood risks have the same optimum, so teacher forcing is globally optimal for fitting observed sequence distributions in that idealized setting.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 2 uses surjectivity of the score map and the fact that any sequence-level R can place its score at EOS to equate the minima of L_ARM(q), L_EBM(R_r), and L_EBM(R). The construction recovers the optimal sequence distribution as a product of teacher-forced next-token conditionals. The proposition says nothing about whether finite causal Transformers, SGD, or finite data reach that optimum.

anchors.section: 4.1 Proposition 2 and Optimality of teacher forcing

key_findings.claim: The practical approximation guarantee is a horizon-linear uniform-logit bound, not a guarantee that ordinary next-token training will find the required future value.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 3 bounds either KL direction by 2T times the maximum absolute difference between q and q*=M(r) over all relevant prefix-state/token pairs. A cited causal-Transformer universality result yields 2T epsilon when q* is uniformly approximated, but requires embedding dimension to scale with vocabulary. The premise demands a worst-case approximation over an exponentially large prefix set and can be much stronger than low average teacher-forced loss.

key_findings.claim: The exact-enumeration experiments reproduce equal or very similar EBM and ARM optimization behavior, but only in tiny synthetic sequence spaces.
key_findings.evidence: The experiments enumerate all 4,096 sequences for V=8,T=4 and all 65,536 for V=4,T=8, use fixed-length Zipf or softargmax-normal target distributions, and train matched causal/non-causal Transformers with 3,633 or 76,609 parameters. Figures 2-4 show the expected-risk gaps for ARM and EBM falling to similar levels and the mapped logits approaching each other; no natural language, pretrained model, long horizon, or approximate partition computation is involved.

key_findings.claim: The paper's own peaked-target experiment shows that distributional agreement does not imply uniform agreement of the underlying logits.
key_findings.evidence: In Figure 5's softargmax-normal targets at temperature 0.1, KL approaches zero while the post-mapping L-infinity logit distance remains large. The authors explain that softargmax's inverse is not Lipschitz near a simplex vertex: very different scores can induce nearly the same highly concentrated distribution. This qualifies any interpretation of the score bijection as identifiable from data.

anchors.section: C.5 Bounding KL divergence by logits distance

key_findings.claim: Across the displayed learning-rate sweep the ARM is slightly more robust, while the reported gradient-noise statistics are broadly similar between ARM and EBM.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 6-7 show both model classes attaining their best final loss at the same learning rate, with the ARM degrading less at some misspecified rates. Figure 8 compares gradient-noise scale, coherence, and coordinate-wise signal-to-noise and reports similar sensitivity. Exact numeric tables, batch-size details for the noise study, repeat counts, and uncertainty are absent.

key_findings.claim: The printed proof of Proposition 3 reverses the KL arguments, so its displayed chain-rule equality and final substitution are false as written even though the stated inequality is repairable.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B.4 begins with KL(p_q,p_q*) but expands token KL as KL(pi_q*,pi_q) under prefixes sampled from q*, which is the chain rule for KL(p_q*,p_q). It then writes KL(p_q,p_Rr)=KL(p_M(r),p_q), again swapping arguments rather than substituting p_Rr=p_M(r). Lemma 1 provides the same 2||q-q*||_infinity upper bound after swapping f and g, so redoing the chain rule in the correct orientation recovers both directional bounds; the proof text itself nevertheless contains a genuine orientation error.

key_findings.claim: The variable-length sequence definitions are off by one across the main text and appendix.
key_findings.evidence: The main notation defines responses as union_{t=1}^{T-1} V^t followed by EOS, which permits total lengths 2 through T. Appendix A.1 instead maps V^{<=T} to union_{t=1}^{T}(V^t followed by EOS), whose total lengths are 2 through T+1 despite saying length includes EOS. Proposition 4 then uses union_{tau=1}^{T} V^{tau-1} followed by EOS, total lengths 1 through T. The validity proof follows Proposition 4's convention, but the three stated sample spaces are not identical.

anchors.section: A.1 Implicit length handling and Proposition 4

key_findings.claim: Proposition 2's use of minima for any joint data distribution needs a support or extended-score qualification.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines model distributions with full support and finite real-valued score spaces, yet says NLL is zero iff a conditional probability equals one and states minima for any rho. If rho is deterministic or has zero-probability sequences, finite softmax scores cannot attain the boundary distribution; the optimum is an infimum approached by diverging logits. The equality of optimal values remains conceptually correct with full-support rho, extended-real logits, closure, or 'inf' in place of 'min,' but the unqualified statement is too broad.

key_findings.claim: The paper establishes representational lookahead, not explicit planning or future search at autoregressive inference time.
key_findings.evidence: At the exact optimum, each local q score already contains V_q of all continuations, so ancestral sampling uses future information compressed into the learned conditional. But computing that potential directly from an EBM is exponential, and the paper supplies no scalable conversion or large-model training result. Its conclusion appropriately locates observed teacher-forcing failures in approximation or optimization, but the theorem alone cannot show that a trained LLM has learned the required value function.

anchors.section: Limitations of teacher forcing and paper limitations
A.9 Irrelevance of forward variables for sampling

method.core_idea: Start from the chain-rule bijection between a joint sequence distribution and its next-token conditionals, express both sides through Gibbs scores, and identify the future log-partition correction that converts a global EBM energy into locally normalized autoregressive logits.
method.mechanism: For finite vocabulary V and maximum response length T, an EBM assigns p(y|x) proportional to exp R(x,y), while an ARM multiplies softmax conditionals from local logits q(s_t,y_t). Any sequence reward is written without loss as R_r=sum_t r(s_t,y_t), placing all reward at EOS if necessary. Backward marginalization defines q=M(r): q=r at EOS and q=r+V_q(next prefix) otherwise. The inverse subtracts that future value. Products telescope, yielding identical distributions and equating the EBM global log-partition with the ARM root soft value. The recursion is the deterministic finite-horizon soft Bellman equation and backward DP on a prefix tree. Negative-log-likelihood risks are then compared in unrestricted function space; local softmax stability plus the KL chain rule yields a 2T uniform-logit approximation bound. Tiny Transformers and exact enumeration numerically compare risk convergence, mapped logits, learning-rate sensitivity, and gradient noise.
assumptions: The vocabulary and maximum response horizon are finite, making the sequence sample space and EBM partition function mathematically well defined.
EOS conventions and terminal logits are specified consistently enough to make the ARM a normalized distribution over finished responses.
The EBM reward can be decomposed across prefix actions; arbitrary sequence rewards use a terminal-only decomposition.
For the exact bijection, q and r range over unrestricted tabular score functions on every valid prefix and token.
Function-space results are interpreted modulo softmax gauge freedoms even though the explicit map selects particular score representatives.
Teacher-forcing data identify the desired conditional distribution and have enough support; boundary distributions may require extended-real logits or limits.
For neural approximation, a causal Transformer has sufficient width, embedding dimension, context, and optimization access to uniformly approximate q*=M(r).
A worst-case logit error over all prefix states is a meaningful control quantity for sequence KL.
The finite-horizon prefix process is acyclic with deterministic token-appending transitions and discount gamma=1.
The synthetic exact-enumeration behavior is informative about, but not representative of, large pretrained language-model optimization.
In KL-regularized alignment, the reference policy has full support so its log probability can serve as a reference energy.
Calling the learned conditional 'lookahead' refers to future value encoded in logits, not an explicit inference-time tree search.

techniques.role: Maps a full sequence distribution to unique next-token conditionals by backward marginalization and conditioning.
Adds the next prefix's log-partition to immediate reward so locally normalized logits reproduce a globally normalized energy.
Interprets the score map as a deterministic finite-horizon maximum-entropy RL Bellman equation.
Computes the root log-partition by backward log-sum-exp over the sequence prefix tree.
Uses the score-map surjectivity to equate ideal EBM and ARM negative-log-likelihood optima.
Frames KL-regularized language-model alignment as approximating a reference-weighted EBM with an ancestral-sampling ARM.
Lifts local conditional-distribution error to sequence-level KL along autoregressive trajectories.
Controls either KL direction by 2T times the worst prefix-token score error.
Forces termination at the maximum horizon and proves total probability over finished responses is one.
Identifies the ARM soft value with the EBM backward variable and shows the past forward factor cancels from conditional sampling.
Makes the EBM partition, expected risk, mapped logits, and distributional KL exact in the tiny numerical study.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic fixed-length sequences with V=8, T=4 (4,096 sequences), a two-block pre-layer-norm Transformer with 3,633 parameters, causal mask for ARM and no mask plus mean pooling for EBM.
evaluations.metric: Exact expected NLL optimality gap and centered L-infinity distance from ARM logits to optimal EBM logits before and after M mapping.
evaluations.result: Figure 2 shows ARM and EBM risk curves converging to the same or nearly identical level; after mapping, logit distance falls toward zero while the naive pre-mapping score comparison does not.
evaluations.baseline: Matched non-causal EBM versus causal ARM trained with the same selected Adam learning rate.

evaluations.setting: V=8,T=4 with two-block 3,633-parameter and three-block 76,609-parameter Transformers under a Zipf target distribution.
evaluations.metric: Exact risk gap and mapped/unmapped logit distance over 5,000 optimization steps.
evaluations.result: Appendix Figure 3 reports the same qualitative convergence for under- and over-parameterized variants; exact values, repeats, and error bars are not provided.
evaluations.baseline: ARM and EBM at each model size.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic T>V case, V=4,T=8 (65,536 sequences), two- and three-block Transformers.
evaluations.metric: Exact expected-risk gap and centered logit distance.
evaluations.result: Figure 4 again shows similar risk convergence and decreasing post-mapping distance, extending the visual result to a longer horizon but still only eight tokens.
evaluations.baseline: Matched causal ARM and non-causal EBM.

evaluations.setting: V=8,T=4 and V=4,T=8; two or three blocks; Zipf targets and highly peaked softargmax-normal targets at temperature 0.1.
evaluations.metric: Sequence KL between ARM and mapped EBM compared with L-infinity logit distance.
evaluations.result: Figure 5 is consistent with KL being bounded by the scaled uniform score error. For peaked targets, KL goes to zero while score distance stays large, exposing non-identifiability near the simplex boundary.
evaluations.baseline: Distributional KL versus the theorem's stronger logit-space control quantity.

evaluations.setting: Same tiny Transformer setup across searched Adam learning rates 3e-3, 1e-3, and 1e-4 plus neighboring displayed rates.
evaluations.metric: Final exact loss and loss curves by learning rate.
evaluations.result: Figures 6-7 show the same best learning rate for ARM and EBM and somewhat better ARM robustness to misspecification; no numeric table or repeated-run uncertainty is supplied.
evaluations.baseline: Causal ARM versus non-causal EBM at each learning rate.

evaluations.setting: Mini-batch gradient analysis during tiny-model training; the appendix does not state the batch size or repeat protocol.
evaluations.metric: Loss, gradient-noise scale, gradient coherence, and mean coordinate-wise signal-to-noise ratio.
evaluations.result: Figure 8 shows broadly similar ARM and EBM noise sensitivity across steps, with crossing curves rather than uniform dominance.

limitations: [Author-stated] Exact EBM/ARM and teacher-forcing equivalence is proved in unrestricted function space; it does not account for neural approximation or optimization error.
[Author-stated] In practice the EBM can use a non-causal Transformer while the ARM must use a causal one, so their finite architecture classes and learning complexity differ.
[Author-stated] The ARM logit must simultaneously model immediate local score and a potentially complex soft value over every future continuation using a backward-looking architecture.
[Author-stated] Formally comparing the complexity of learning the EBM reward and learning the ARM logits is left open.
[Author-stated] Latent variables or thinking traces as a way to increase ARM expressivity are left for future work.
[Author-stated] The cited causal-Transformer uniform approximation result requires embedding dimension to scale with vocabulary size.

[Reviewer-identified] All experiments use exact enumeration of only 4,096 or 65,536 fixed-length sequences and Transformers with at most 76,609 parameters; no pretrained or natural-language model is tested.
[Reviewer-identified] The exact EBM-to-ARM map costs O(V^T), so the paper does not provide a scalable method for converting a practical global reward into next-token lookahead logits.

[Reviewer-identified] The 2T bound grows with horizon and assumes uniform accuracy over every reachable prefix/token, including exponentially many rare or unseen contexts; ordinary average NLL does not establish this premise.
[Reviewer-identified] Numerical plots provide no seed count, confidence interval, significance test, or numeric result table; details for the gradient-noise mini-batches are incomplete.
[Reviewer-identified] Experiments fix response length and therefore do not test the variable-length/EOS construction proved in the appendix.

[Reviewer-identified] Appendix B.4 reverses both token and sequence KL arguments in the printed proof. The theorem can be repaired by applying the symmetric sup-norm bound in the correct chain-rule orientation, but the given derivation is invalid.

[Reviewer-identified] The response sample space is defined three different ways: the main text, Appendix A.1, and Proposition 4 disagree about inclusion of EOS-only responses and whether maximum total length is T or T+1.

[Reviewer-identified] Proposition 2 states minima for any data distribution despite finite softmax models having full support; distributions with zero-mass sequences generally yield an unattained infimum unless extended logits or closure are allowed.

[Reviewer-identified] The forced terminal score q=-infinity lies outside the declared real-valued function space F(S x A), another boundary convention that needs an extended-real or action-set formulation.

[Reviewer-identified] Equality of representable distributions does not identify a unique learned energy or logit representation because state-wise additive gauges and near-boundary softmax behavior permit very different scores.

[Reviewer-identified] The supervised-risk theorem does not analyze practical RL post-training, where reward samples are adaptive, optimization is policy-constrained, and the target EBM itself may be misspecified or inaccessible.
[Reviewer-identified] Calling the result 'lookahead capabilities' risks conflating future value already encoded in trained logits with explicit inference-time planning or search.
failure_modes: A causal model with insufficient depth, width, context, or training signal can fail to approximate the exponentially structured soft future value even though a tabular q exists.
Teacher forcing can converge to a shortcut or spurious next-token solution under finite data and parameterization, never reaching the function-space optimum invoked by Proposition 2.
Small token-level score errors accumulate with horizon; the 2T guarantee can become loose or vacuous for long responses.
Rare prefixes receive little teacher-forced supervision but are included in the worst-case map and may be visited after an early sampling error.
A highly peaked target can have tiny KL while logits remain far apart, making recovered rewards, values, or score interpretations unstable.
Inconsistent EOS indexing or failure to force termination can leave probability mass on invalid sequences or create off-by-one likelihood errors.
Putting an arbitrary sequence reward only at EOS makes the exact recursion valid but creates extremely delayed credit and an intractable future marginal for learning.
A learned reward or verifier can encode bias, misspecification, or reward hacking; exact ARM distillation would faithfully reproduce the wrong EBM.
Truncated MCMC or approximate EBM samples can train conditionals for the sampler's distribution rather than the intended globally normalized target.
A finite context window merges prefix states and invalidates the full-prefix tree abstraction; an order-W process may not represent distinctions needed by the target energy.
The printed KL-orientation error can be copied into implementations or later analyses, evaluating the wrong expectation and misleading asymmetric-divergence claims.
Matching synthetic exact risk does not ensure planning, reasoning, or alignment performance on natural long-form tasks.
Optimization comparisons can change under unmatched effective capacity, since the EBM attends bidirectionally and the ARM is causally masked.
A reference policy without full support assigns negative-infinite reference energy, breaking finite-score derivations and preventing the aligned policy from reaching excluded sequences.
reusable_insights: Separate representational equivalence from computational conversion and statistical learnability; a bijection can exist while one direction remains exponentially expensive.
Locally normalized autoregressive logits can be understood as an immediate score plus a soft future-value potential.
The chain rule of probability and the soft Bellman equation are two views of the same backward marginalization on a finite sequence tree.
When comparing sequence models, lift token-level KL with the correctly oriented autoregressive chain rule and state which model generates the prefix expectation.
Uniform logit error is a strong sufficient condition for distributional closeness, but peaked softmax distributions show it is far from necessary.
Teacher forcing is not structurally myopic at its unrestricted global optimum; practical myopia can still arise from approximation, optimization, data, and credit-assignment limits.
EOS and maximum-horizon conventions are part of the theorem, not bookkeeping; define content length and total length once and use valid action sets at terminal states.
Backward variables in an EBM are precisely the future quantities that an ancestral sampler must amortize into its conditionals.
Exact enumeration is valuable for validating identities, but claims about LLM training need a second empirical tier where partitions are intractable and models are pretrained.
Near a probability-simplex boundary, evaluate both distribution distance and calibrated score/value error because inverse-softmax interpretations are unstable.
If a theorem is intended for arbitrary empirical distributions, write infima or explicitly allow extended-real logits and zero probabilities.
A practical lookahead claim should distinguish latent value encoded at training time, explicit test-time search, and external reward-guided inference.
open_questions: What architecture, sample, and optimization complexity is required for a causal Transformer to learn q=M(r) compared with a non-causal Transformer learning R?
Can a non-vacuous average-case KL bound replace the worst-prefix L-infinity assumption while controlling rare-prefix exposure under autoregressive sampling?
Do mapped-value signatures appear in real pretrained LLM logits on planning tasks, and can they predict success or failure better than next-token loss?
Can twisted SMC, GFlowNets, or learned critics provide a scalable training target for the future-value term without enumerating V^T continuations?
How do latent reasoning traces change the size or smoothness of the future-value function that the causal model must represent?
Does teacher forcing reach the EBM-equivalent solution on the pathological planning tasks where finite Transformers empirically fail, after capacity and optimization are controlled?
What is the correct theorem for finite context windows where prefixes merge into an order-W Markov state?
How should the bijection be formulated on quotient score spaces so gauge non-identifiability, terminal invalid actions, and extended-real logits are explicit?
Can Proposition 2 be restated with infima and arbitrary-support data distributions, and can Proposition 3's proof be corrected in the official version?
How much does the 2T worst-case bound overestimate actual sequence error for natural heavy-tailed language distributions?
Can an ARM be distilled from a sequence-level reward at LLM scale with measurable bidirectional KL and without on-policy mode collapse?
How do reward-model error and reference-policy support constraints propagate through the EBM-to-ARM interpretation of alignment?
Would matched compute and expressivity comparisons between causal and bidirectional networks reproduce the nearly identical tiny-model learning curves?
Can variable-length experiments verify the EOS construction after resolving the paper's three inconsistent length conventions?

competitive_landscape.title: The pitfalls of next-token prediction
competitive_landscape.difference: The Pitfalls of Next-Token Prediction separates teacher-forced training from autoregressive inference and exhibits planning tasks where finite Transformers and Mamba fail to learn the necessary next-token rule, with multi-token prediction helping. The EBM-bijection paper shows only that teacher forcing has the right unrestricted global optimum; its own limitation section therefore treats those failures as approximation or optimization rather than refuting them empirically.

competitive_landscape.title: Joint Learning of Energy-based Models and their Partition Function
competitive_landscape.difference: This same-author work jointly parameterizes an EBM energy and log-partition, giving a tractable min-min training criterion without MCMC in combinatorial spaces, but still needs difficult EBM sampling. The ARM paper instead shows that teacher-forced conditionals implicitly represent the normalized sequence distribution and focuses on the exact score map and distillation error.

competitive_landscape.title: Probabilistic Inference in Language Models via Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo
competitive_landscape.difference: Twisted SMC learns a future-potential twist and performs approximate sampling from a full-sequence reward distribution, with bidirectional partition/KL bounds and real language-model applications. The bijection identifies the ideal twist-like soft value analytically but offers no scalable EBM-to-ARM conversion or inference algorithm; twisted SMC directly addresses that practical gap with test-time computation.

competitive_landscape.title: Amortizing intractable inference in large language models
competitive_landscape.difference: This work fine-tunes autoregressive LLMs with GFlowNet objectives to amortize intractable posterior sampling for continuation, infilling, constrained generation, and latent chain-of-thought tasks. It provides practical large-model distribution matching, whereas the EBM-bijection paper provides cleaner function-space equivalence and KL theory but validates only tiny exact-enumeration models.

competitive_landscape.title: ShiQ: Bringing back Bellman to LLMs
competitive_landscape.difference: ShiQ derives shifted Q-learning losses that make LLM logits usable as Q-values and demonstrates off-policy token-wise learning on synthetic, preference, and tool-use benchmarks. The EBM paper derives the soft Bellman form from the chain rule and defends teacher-forced likelihood at the ideal optimum; ShiQ is an alternative practical objective for explicitly training the value semantics that the bijection says logits must contain.

competitive_landscape.title: Generative Flow Networks as Entropy-Regularized RL
competitive_landscape.difference: This work already casts GFlowNet sampling on general construction DAGs as entropy-regularized RL and applies standard soft-RL algorithms. The EBM paper specializes the connection to language prefix trees, derives an explicit invertible ARM/EBM score map from the probability chain rule, and adds supervised-risk equivalence and a logit-to-KL bound.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim an exact ARM-EBM bijection in function space, identify it as a special case of the soft Bellman equation, prove equal supervised-learning minima and an EBM-to-ARM KL approximation bound, and use these results to explain how next-token predictors can look ahead.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper gives explicit forward and inverse local-score formulas, telescoping and variational proofs, MaxEnt-RL, dynamic-programming, and probabilistic-inference derivations, Proposition 2 on ideal NLL optima, Proposition 3's 2T uniform-logit bound, and exact tiny-model experiments. Prior work already established soft Bellman/maximum-entropy RL, GFlowNet-as-RL, global-energy probabilistic inference, learned future twists, and empirical teacher-forcing failures; the paper itself acknowledges these connections. The printed KL proof has an argument-order error, and the support and EOS conventions need qualification, but the core distributional identity and a corrected two-direction bound remain sound.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest novelty is the unusually explicit synthesis: deriving an invertible local-score map directly from the chain rule and using it to connect EBM likelihood, teacher forcing, and soft value functions in one finite-sequence formalism. The result clarifies that next-token likelihood is not representationally myopic at an unrestricted global optimum. It does not establish that real LLMs learn or execute planning, does not make EBM-to-ARM conversion tractable, and does not overturn finite-model counterexamples; those are precisely approximation, optimization, and computational questions left open.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text review of every page of the pinned 32-page arXiv v4/ICML 2026 version, including all propositions, proofs, variable-length derivations, forward-backward identities, pseudocode, and Figures 1-8. The contradiction audit independently checked KL orientation in Appendix B.4, the three incompatible EOS/length sample spaces, and the unattained-minimum issue for non-full-support data; these are formal presentation/proof defects, not grounds to discard the core chain-rule bijection. Numerical claims are qualitative where plots provide no exact table or uncertainty. Competitive titles, canonical IDs, latest arXiv revisions, and dates were checked against official arXiv version histories on 2026-08-23. This record remains full_text and does not claim secondary verification.
